_about: The Fair value appendix's plain-language guide (fairvalue-view.js loads it): valuation from zero, start-up valuation, every abbreviation in full with a plain explanation, and for each method what it is, why it works, which companies it fits and what to watch; what each stage means and why it weights the methods as it does. Static text: the per-company reasons come from app/valuation_methods.py (appendix 'fit').

primer.title: Valuation from zero
paras: A share is a small slice of ownership in a company. Its price is what buyers and sellers agree on today; its value is an estimate of what that slice is really worth. Valuation means estimating the value from the company's own numbers and comparing it with the price. When the estimate is well above the price the share looks cheap, when it is below it looks expensive — always within a wide margin of error.

The core idea: a business is worth the cash it will hand to its owners over its whole life. Cash later is worth less than cash now, because money in hand can be invested, prices rise, and the future may never arrive. So future cash is shrunk, or “discounted”, at a rate that grows with the risk. That rate is the cost of capital: the yearly return investors demand for putting money into this company instead of somewhere safer.

The methods fall into four families. Cash-flow (intrinsic) methods forecast the cash and discount it: DCF, owner earnings, residual income, dividend models. Relative methods price the company like similar companies through multiples such as P/E or EV/Sales. Asset methods ask what would be left if the business stopped: net cash, tangible book, liquidation value. Probability methods run thousands of scenarios or weigh success against failure: Monte Carlo, regime switching, survival weighting. Reference figures — analysts' price targets, prediction markets, the trading range — are shown for comparison and are not valuations.

No single method is right. Each rests on assumptions and has blind spots, so the page shows them side by side (the football field), and the spread between them is information in itself. Which methods count most depends on the company's stage: a cash-burning start-up, a mature dividend payer and a bank need different tools. The weights are fixed in the code before any result is seen, so no method is chosen because it gives a pleasing answer.

From the whole company to one share: methods that value the entire business give the enterprise value (EV), the value of the operations to everyone who funded them. Subtract debt and other claims, add cash, and what is left is the equity value — the owners' part — which is divided by the diluted share count to give a value per share.

How to read each method below: “What it is” explains it from the start; “Why it works” gives the reasoning behind it; “Fits” says which companies it suits; “Watch out” lists its blind spots; “Why it applies here” uses this company's own figures. Then come the formula, the same formula with this company's numbers in it, the inputs with their sources (usually the company's own SEC filings) and the assumptions with their basis. Every abbreviation is written out in full under “Terms”, and all of them are in the glossary.

startups.title: Valuing start-ups and pre-profit companies
paras: Young companies break the usual tools. With no profit, a P/E ratio has nothing to divide by. A DCF of a loss-making business mostly restates the forecaster's hopes, because almost all of its value lies in a distant future its short history cannot vouch for. Many start-ups fail outright, and those that succeed usually raise more money first, which splits the ownership into more pieces (dilution). A start-up valuation has to handle all three: the path to profit, the chance of failure and the dilution along the way.

Private investors use a handful of standard approaches. The venture capital (VC) method estimates what the company could be worth in about five years and discounts that back at a very high target return; commonly cited ranges run from about 50–70% a year at the start-up stage to 25–35% just before a public listing, because the rate also has to pay for the many investments that fail. The First Chicago method weighs a success, a middling and a failure scenario by their probabilities. The Berkus and scorecard methods, used for pre-revenue seed rounds, score the idea, the team, the prototype and the market by judgment. Option-pricing methods divide the value among share classes when the funding structure is complex.

What this site uses, and why. It works only from public filings and prices, so it uses the methods those can feed: net cash (floor) and the market-implied value of the pipeline for pre-revenue companies; the path-to-margin DCF with dilution; the exit-multiple method, which is the VC method with public-market inputs; the survival-weighted value, a two-scenario First Chicago method with the failure probability taken from distress models or the cash runway; and EV/Sales against the Rule of 40, which prices growth plus cash generation across all listed companies. Berkus and scorecard are not used: they need judgments about the team and the product that no filing contains.

The numbers to watch at this stage: the burn rate (cash used per year), the cash runway (how many years the cash lasts at that rate), the dilution needed to reach break-even, the Rule of 40 score, and how much of the market value is a bet on the future rather than on the business as it is today.
classic: Venture capital (VC) method
Exit value in about five years ÷ (1 + target return)^years. The target return is very high because it also pays for the investments that fail.
Used as the exit-multiple (venture) method, with peer margins and P/E from public markets and failure handled separately by survival weighting.
First Chicago method
Probability-weighted scenarios: success, middling, failure.
Used in reduced form as the survival-weighted value: going concern vs liquidation, with a stated failure probability.
Berkus method
Adds a fixed amount for each risk an early company has reduced: a sound idea, a prototype, a quality team, strategic relationships, a product rollout or sales.
Not used: it needs judgments about the team and the product that filings do not contain.
Scorecard method
Starts from the average pre-money value of similar funded start-ups and adjusts it by weighted scores for team, market size, product, competition and so on.
Not used: needs private-round data and qualitative scores.
Option pricing (OPM)
Treats each share class as an option on the company's value to split value among preferred and common shares.
Not used: listed companies here have one common class whose price is observed.
Discounted cash flow (DCF) with a path to profit
Forecasts the losses, the turn to profit and the cash after it, and adds the dilution from funding the losses.
Used: path-to-margin DCF, dilution-adjusted.
Revenue multiples
Prices the company on its sales like similar companies, since there are no profits to price.
Used: EV/Sales vs peers and EV/Sales vs Rule of 40.

pre_revenue.label: Pre-revenue
pre_revenue.means: Almost no revenue yet (under $25 million over four quarters) and an operating loss: a drug in trials, a product not yet launched. The value is a pipeline that no filing can price.
pre_revenue.why: With nothing to forecast from, the weight goes to what can be measured: the cash on hand (net cash, 50%) and the assets (tangible book, 30%), plus the survival-weighted value (20%), which accounts for the chance the company runs out of money. The price above these floors is what the market pays for the pipeline.

pre_profit.label: Pre-profit / high growth
pre_profit.means: An operating loss, but revenue growing 10% a year or more: a young company scaling up.
pre_profit.why: The value depends on whether and when margins turn positive and how much the owners are diluted before then, so the path-to-margin DCF with dilution (25%), the survival-weighted value (20%) and the venture exit-multiple method (20%) lead, checked by how the market prices growth across all companies (Rule of 40, 15%) and by peers' sales multiples (20%).

high_growth.label: High growth
high_growth.means: Profitable, with revenue growing 20% a year or more.
high_growth.why: Profits make a DCF possible, but its long-range growth is fragile, so the company's own DCF (25%) is paired with an outside view of what similar companies actually achieved (25%), the Rule of 40 fit (15%) and peers' multiples of sales (15%) and earnings (20%).

growth.label: Growth
growth.means: Profitable, with revenue growing 8–20% a year.
growth.why: Growth is steady enough for a cash-flow forecast to carry the most weight (DCF 35%), tempered by base rates (25%) and by what peers trade at on earnings (P/E 25%) and on EBITDA (15%).

mature.label: Mature
mature.means: Profitable, with revenue growing 0–8% a year: an established business.
mature.why: Its value is mostly cash generated now, so cash-flow methods (DCF 25%, owner earnings 20%), the cash actually returned to shareholders (15%) and peer multiples (P/E 25%, EV/EBITDA 15%) share the weight.

cyclical.label: Cyclical
cyclical.means: Profits that swing with the economy or commodity prices — mining, energy, chemicals, metals, autos, semiconductors, airlines, homebuilders, shipping — or a quarterly operating margin that varies by more than 8 points.
cyclical.why: This year's profit may be a peak or a trough, so the methods use a mid-cycle margin — the median since 2020 — instead: normalized P/E (35%), normalized DCF (35%) and EV/EBITDA against peers (30%).

decline.label: Decline / turnaround
decline.means: An operating loss with little growth, or revenue falling over one year and over three years.
decline.why: The question becomes what is left: tangible book (30%) as an asset floor, sales against peers (25%) and survival (20%), with smaller weights on the DCF (10%) and owner earnings (15%) in case a turnaround works.

financial.label: Financial (bank / insurer)
financial.means: A bank or an insurer. Its raw material is money: deposits, loans, premiums and investments.
financial.why: A bank's cash flows cannot be separated from its financing, so its tools are built on book value and the return on it: residual income, price-to-book against return on equity across peers, the justified multiple from the Gordon growth model, and dividends.

reit.label: REIT
reit.means: A real estate investment trust, which must pay out at least 90% of its taxable income as dividends.
reit.why: Depreciation on buildings understates a REIT's earnings, so funds from operations (FFO) is the standard measure: P/FFO against other REITs (55%), the dividend model (20%) and residual income on book value (25%).

glossary.plain: What one share last traded for on the stock exchange.
Share price × the number of shares: what the market says the whole company's equity is worth today.

The value of the business itself, to everyone who funded it: market value + debt + other claims − cash. Two companies with the same operations but different debt have different market values but similar EVs.
The owners' share of the business: EV − debt − other claims + cash. Divided by shares, it is the value per share.
Debt minus cash (plus other claims here). Negative net debt means the company holds more cash than it owes: net cash.
Cash and investments minus debt and other claims: money the company could hand back if it stopped tomorrow.
Parts of the company owned by someone other than its common shareholders — outside owners of subsidiaries, holders of preferred shares — which must be subtracted before the common shares' value.
Shares outstanding plus those that options, restricted stock and convertible securities would add. Using it avoids overstating the value per share.
When a company issues new shares, each existing share owns a smaller slice. Loss-making companies often fund themselves this way.
Money customers paid for the company's products and services in the period, before any costs.
Revenue minus the costs of running the business (production, staff, research, marketing, depreciation), before interest and taxes. It shows whether the core business makes money.
Close to operating income: profit from the business before the cost of its debt and before tax.

glossary.full: Earnings before interest, taxes, depreciation and amortization
glossary.plain: Operating profit with the non-cash charges for wear and tear (depreciation) and for intangible assets (amortization) added back: a rough measure of cash profit before financing and reinvestment.

The accounting charge that spreads the cost of equipment, buildings (depreciation) and intangible assets such as software or patents (amortization) over the years they are used. It is an expense, but no cash leaves in that year.
What is left of revenue after every cost, interest and tax: the profit that belongs to shareholders.
Net income ÷ diluted shares: the profit belonging to one share.
A profit as a share of revenue. An operating margin of 20% means 20 cents of operating profit on each dollar of sales.
Income tax as a share of pretax income. Here, the company's own rate when it is between 0 and 35%, else the US federal rate of 21%.
Pay given to employees in shares or options instead of cash. It costs shareholders through dilution even though no cash is paid.
Cash the business actually brought in from its operations in the period, from the cash-flow statement.
Cash spent on long-lived assets: factories, equipment, data centers, software. It keeps the business running and growing.
Cash tied up in, or released from, the day-to-day cycle of inventory, money owed by customers (receivables) and bills owed to suppliers (payables). A growing company usually ties up more.
Cash left after running the business and paying for the investment it needs (operating cash minus capex). It is what could go to owners and lenders.

glossary.full: Free cash flow to the firm
glossary.plain: Free cash flow before any payments to lenders: EBIT × (1 − tax rate) + D&A − capex − ΔWC. It belongs to everyone who funded the company, so it is discounted at the WACC to give EV.
Operating profit after tax, as if the company had no debt: EBIT × (1 − tax rate).
Net income + D&A − capex: roughly the cash an owner could take out each year without shrinking the business. A measure described by Warren Buffett.
How much cash a loss-making company uses per year (negative free cash flow).
How many years the cash would last at the current burn rate: cash ÷ yearly cash burn.
Assets minus liabilities on the balance sheet: the money shareholders put in plus the profits the company kept. Recorded mostly at historical cost, not market prices.
Book value minus goodwill and other intangible assets: the part of the shareholders' money that sits in physical and financial assets that could be sold.
The premium a company paid over the book value of businesses it bought. It cannot be sold on its own.
Non-physical assets such as patents, brands, customer lists and software that a company bought or recorded on its balance sheet.
What the assets would fetch in a forced sale if the company closed. Here, tangible book × 0.8.
The value of the company assuming it keeps operating, as opposed to being wound up.
Net income ÷ shareholders' equity: how much profit the company earns on each dollar of the owners' money.
Net income ÷ tangible book value: ROE without goodwill and intangibles. The standard profitability measure for banks.
NOPAT ÷ the capital invested in the business (debt + equity − cash). It shows how much each dollar put into the business earns; growth only adds value when ROIC is above the WACC.
Converting future cash into today's money: cash in n years ÷ (1 + rate)^n. At 10% a year, $110 next year is worth $100 today.

The return the company must earn to satisfy all its funders: the cost of equity and the after-tax cost of debt, weighted by how much of each it uses (at market values). It is the discount rate for cash flows that belong to the whole firm.
The yearly return shareholders demand for owning this stock, given its risk. Estimated here with CAPM.
The interest rate the company pays on its borrowing. Interest is tax-deductible, so its after-tax cost is k_d × (1 − tax rate).
The shares of equity and debt in the company's funding, at market values; they weight the two costs in the WACC.
The standard formula for the cost of equity: risk-free rate + beta × equity risk premium. Investors are paid only for the risk they cannot diversify away, which beta measures.
The return on an investment with (almost) no risk of loss; here the 10-year US Treasury yield.
The extra yearly return investors demand for owning stocks instead of Treasuries. A fixed long-run assumption here.
How much a stock tends to move when the market moves. A beta of 1.5 means it has typically moved 1.5% for each 1% of the market (here the S&P 500 ETF, SPY), measured on weekly returns.
Measured betas drift toward 1 over time, so the estimate is pulled two-thirds of the way to it: 0.67 × measured beta + 0.33. Named after Marshall Blume, who documented the drift.
How much of one thing's variation a fitted line explains, from 0 (nothing) to 1 (everything). A beta with a low R² is a noisy estimate.
Forecast the cash a business will produce and discount it back to today. The basic method of intrinsic valuation.
In a DCF, the value of all the years after the explicit forecast (here year 5), summarized in one figure that assumes steady growth forever. It is often most of the total value.
The yearly rate at which cash flows are assumed to grow forever after the forecast. It must stay below the economy's long-run growth and below the discount rate.

The value of a cash flow that grows forever at rate g, discounted at rate k: next year's cash ÷ (k − g). Named after the economist Myron Gordon; it underlies terminal values, the dividend discount model and justified multiples.
The steady yearly growth rate that would take a figure from its starting value to its ending value over a period.
A price divided by a measure of the business — earnings, sales, book. Comparing multiples across similar companies is relative valuation.
Share price ÷ earnings per share: how many years of today's profit the price pays for.
Enterprise value ÷ EBITDA. Compares companies regardless of how much debt they carry or how they depreciate assets.
Enterprise value ÷ revenue. Usable even when there is no profit.
Market value ÷ book value. Above 1, investors expect the company to earn more than investors demand on its equity.
Market value ÷ tangible book value. The standard multiple for banks.
A REIT's net income plus real-estate depreciation minus gains on property sales, as defined by Nareit: closer to its recurring cash earnings than net income.
Market value ÷ FFO: the REIT equivalent of a P/E.
The cash dividend paid on one share over a year.
Dividends ÷ net income: the share of profit paid out. What is kept (1 − payout) funds growth.
Values a share as the discounted stream of its future dividends; with steady growth it is DPS × (1 + g) ÷ (kₑ − g).
Cash a company spends buying back its own shares, which raises each remaining share's slice of the company.
Dividends plus buybacks over a year, as a share of market value: the cash returned to owners.
Profit above the return shareholders require on their capital: net income − cost of equity × book value. Value is created only when it is positive.
The part of the price paid for future growth: market value minus what today's earnings would be worth if they never grew (earnings ÷ cost of equity).
Valuing each business segment separately and adding them up, for companies whose divisions deserve different multiples.
A rule of thumb from growth investing: revenue growth % + free-cash-flow margin % should be at least 40. It lets fast growth make up for losses and vice versa.
The similar companies a multiple is taken from: the narrowest SIC industry group with at least six covered companies.
The US government's four-digit industry codes; the SEC assigns one to every filer (for example 7372, prepackaged software).
The middle value when numbers are sorted: half are above it, half below. Less swayed by extremes than an average.
The 25th and 75th percentiles; between them lies the middle half of the peers.
Run the same calculation thousands of times with inputs drawn at random from realistic ranges, and look at the spread of the results instead of one number. Named after the casino.
The 10th percentile is the value 10% of scenarios fall below; the 90th, the value 90% fall below. Between them lies the middle 80% of outcomes.
A measure of how spread out numbers are around their average. A margin with a σ of 8 points typically swings about 8 points up or down.
A line fitted through many companies' data to describe how one measure relates to another, such as EV/Sales and the Rule of 40 score.
How far a fitted estimate typically misses; ±1 standard error gives a range around the fitted value.
A scale that turns multiplication into addition, so that a doubling counts the same at any size; used because multiples are skewed.
A model in which the next state (here a growth regime) depends only on the current one, through a table of switching probabilities.
A spell of similar behaviour — high growth, steady, decline — that a company can switch between.
Forecasting from what usually happens to similar cases (the base rate) rather than from the details of this one; it corrects the optimism of inside-view forecasts.
Profit at a typical point of the business cycle rather than at a peak or trough; here, the median margin since 2020.
A business whose profits rise and fall with the economy or commodity prices.
Products still in development — drugs in trials, technology not yet sold — that may produce revenue later.
The estimated chance the company fails to pay its debts or goes bankrupt within a period, from credit models on the Credit section.
Extra yearly return growth investors demand from young, unproven companies on top of the CAPM cost of equity. Here 5 points, an assumption.
How much a method counts in the stage-weighted value, fixed by the company's stage before any result is seen.
The chart of horizontal bars, one per method, showing each value range against the share price; named for its look.
Claims plus underwriting costs ÷ premiums earned. Below 100% the insurer profits from underwriting itself, before investment income.
A company that owns income-producing property and must pay out at least 90% of its taxable income as dividends.
The machine-readable tags companies attach to the numbers in their SEC filings; the site reads its figures from them.
The financial reports US-listed companies file with the Securities and Exchange Commission (SEC).
The US regulator that receives company filings; its EDGAR system publishes them.
Where a Wall Street analyst expects the share price to be in about 12 months. Targets tend to follow the price and lean optimistic.
A market where people bet on outcomes, including ranges for a stock's price; contract prices read as the crowd's probabilities.
The lowest and highest closing prices over the past year.
Money invested in young private companies in exchange for shares, by funds that expect most bets to fail and a few to pay for all of them.
A way to split a start-up's value among share classes by treating each as an option on the company's value.
An exchange-traded fund that tracks the S&P 500 index of large US companies; used as “the market” when measuring beta.
A fund that holds a basket of securities and trades on an exchange like a single stock.
The St. Louis Fed's public database of economic series; DGS10 is its series for the 10-year Treasury yield.

glossary.full: Electronic Data Gathering, Analysis, and Retrieval
glossary.plain: The SEC's system where companies file their reports and anyone can read them.
Greenwald's value of a business that never grows: normalized after-tax operating profit (plus depreciation, less upkeep capital spending) divided by the cost of capital.
Current assets minus all liabilities: what is left for shareholders from working capital alone. A 'net-net' trades below two-thirds of it.
P/E divided by the expected growth rate in percent; PEGY adds the dividend yield to the growth. About 1 is "fair" by Peter Lynch's rule.
The cash left for shareholders after the business has reinvested and after net borrowing: what could be paid out as dividends and buybacks.

The yearly return a buyer at today's price earns if a model's forecast comes true — the discount rate that makes the model's value equal the price. Compare it with the cost of equity: above it, the price leaves room.

The 1973 formula for the value of an option from the underlying value, the strike, the time left, the risk-free rate and the volatility. A real option applies it to a business decision instead of a traded stock.
What the safest US corporate bonds pay; the Graham formula scales values by it (FRED series DAAA).
The right, but not the obligation, to make a business decision later — expand, delay, abandon — valued like a financial option.
Buildings, machines, land and other physical assets, at cost less depreciation (the balance sheet line).

DCF — Monte Carlo 10th–90th percentile.what: Discounted cash flow (DCF) forecasts the free cash flow the business will produce — the cash left after running it and reinvesting in it — for five years, adds a terminal value for all the years after, and shrinks each year's cash back to today at the weighted average cost of capital (WACC). The sum is the enterprise value; minus debt and other claims, plus cash, divided by diluted shares, it is a value per share. The Monte Carlo part reruns the DCF thousands of times with growth, margins, the WACC and terminal growth drawn from realistic ranges, and shows the 10th to 90th percentile of the results.
DCF — Monte Carlo 10th–90th percentile.why: It values the business the way an owner would: by the cash it produces, adjusted for when that cash arrives and how risky it is. It is the reference method of intrinsic valuation; most multiples are shortcuts for it.
DCF — Monte Carlo 10th–90th percentile.fits: Companies with positive operating income, so that there are margins to project. Weighted most for growth (35%) and mature companies; for high-growth companies it is checked by the outside view and peers.
DCF — Monte Carlo 10th–90th percentile.watch: Small changes in the WACC or in terminal growth move the value a lot, and the terminal value is often most of the total. On a loss-making company it only restates its assumptions, so it is not used there.

Regime-switching Monte Carlo 10th–90th.what: A ten-year Monte Carlo in which revenue growth switches between regimes — high growth, steady, decline — following a Markov chain: a table of the chances of moving from one regime to another each year, estimated from this company's history and a panel of other companies. Margins drift with the regime, and each path's cash is discounted as in a DCF, net of stock-based compensation.
Regime-switching Monte Carlo 10th–90th.why: Companies do not grow at one smooth rate; they have good runs and bad spells. Letting each path switch regimes gives a more honest spread of outcomes than one straight-line forecast.
Regime-switching Monte Carlo 10th–90th.fits: Companies with a DCF and enough revenue history to estimate the switching.
Regime-switching Monte Carlo 10th–90th.watch: The switching table comes from the past; a company that changes its business can behave unlike its history. Read the range, not just the median.

Outside view — base-rate Monte Carlo.what: The same DCF, but with growth, margins, the WACC and terminal growth drawn from what companies in the same industry and size class actually achieved since 2010, instead of from this company's own trend.
Outside view — base-rate Monte Carlo.why: Forecasts built from one company's recent record tend to be too optimistic. Research on forecasting, notably by Daniel Kahneman, shows that starting from the base rates of similar cases — the outside view — corrects much of that bias.
Outside view — base-rate Monte Carlo.fits: Every company with a DCF; weighted heavily for high-growth and growth companies, where optimism costs most.
Outside view — base-rate Monte Carlo.watch: A company can genuinely differ from its peers — a new category leader, say — and the outside view will then undervalue it.

P/E vs peers.what: Price-to-earnings (P/E) is the share price divided by earnings per share (EPS): how many dollars investors pay for one dollar of yearly profit. This method takes the median P/E of similar companies (the narrowest SIC industry group with at least six of them) and multiplies it by this company's EPS; the peers' middle half gives the range.
P/E vs peers.why: If similar businesses trade at about 20 times earnings, a company with similar prospects should too. It captures what the market is willing to pay today, which a DCF does not.
P/E vs peers.fits: Profitable companies with enough peers; part of most stages.
P/E vs peers.watch: It inherits any mispricing of the whole peer group, and EPS can be bent by one-off items, buybacks and tax. Peers may differ in growth and risk.

EV/EBITDA vs peers.what: EBITDA is earnings before interest, taxes, depreciation and amortization: operating profit with the non-cash charges added back. EV/EBITDA divides enterprise value by it. The method applies the peers' median multiple to this company's EBITDA to get an enterprise value, subtracts net debt and divides by diluted shares.
EV/EBITDA vs peers.why: Built on enterprise value, it compares companies whatever their debt, and it is not affected by different depreciation policies.
EV/EBITDA vs peers.fits: Profitable companies, especially capital-heavy and cyclical ones.
EV/EBITDA vs peers.watch: It ignores the capital spending needed to keep the business running, so a company that must reinvest heavily looks cheaper than it is.

EV/Sales vs peers.what: EV/Sales divides enterprise value by revenue. Applying the peers' median to this company's revenue, then subtracting net debt, gives a value per share from sales alone.
EV/Sales vs peers.why: Revenue exists even when profit does not, so this is the main relative method for young and loss-making companies, and a cross-check for the rest.
EV/Sales vs peers.fits: Every company with revenue and six peers; weighted at the pre-profit, high-growth and decline stages.
EV/Sales vs peers.watch: A dollar of sales at a 5% margin is worth far less than one at 40%; the method assumes this company turns sales into profit like its peers.

Residual income.what: Book value is what shareholders have put into the company plus the profits it kept. Residual income is the profit above the return shareholders require on that book: net income − cost of equity × book. The value is today's book plus the discounted residual income of the next ten years, with the return on equity (ROE) fading to the cost of equity and half of earnings retained.
Residual income.why: A company creates value only when it earns more on its capital than investors demand. Anchoring on book value keeps most of the value in today's balance sheet rather than in distant forecasts.
Residual income.fits: Companies with positive equity and profit; a core method for banks, insurers and REITs, whose balance sheet is their business.
Residual income.watch: Book value can be distorted by buybacks, write-offs and acquisitions; it does not work with negative or tiny equity.

Owner earnings capitalized.what: Owner earnings, a measure described by Warren Buffett, are net income + depreciation and amortization − capital spending: roughly the cash an owner could take out each year without shrinking the business. Capitalizing them means dividing next year's figure by (cost of equity − growth): the value of a cash stream that grows forever at a steady rate.
Owner earnings capitalized.why: For a business that no longer needs heavy reinvestment, today's cash earnings are a sound base, and a steady perpetuity is a fair description of its future.
Owner earnings capitalized.fits: Mature and declining companies with positive owner earnings.
Owner earnings capitalized.watch: It treats all capital spending as upkeep; for a growing company part of it is investment for growth, so owner earnings come out too low. Sensitive to the gap between the cost of equity and growth.

Shareholder yield (dividends + buybacks).what: The cash a company actually returned over the last year — dividends plus share buybacks — valued as a stream growing at the terminal rate and discounted at the cost of equity.
Shareholder yield (dividends + buybacks).why: Cash paid out is the most concrete return an owner receives; a company that returns cash steadily can be valued on that flow.
Shareholder yield (dividends + buybacks).fits: Mature companies that pay dividends or buy back shares.
Shareholder yield (dividends + buybacks).watch: Buybacks are irregular and can be funded with debt; a company paying out more than it earns cannot keep it up.

Normalized (mid-cycle) P/E.what: Replaces this year's earnings with mid-cycle earnings — the median quarterly net margin since 2020 applied to current revenue, per share — and values them at the peer median P/E.
Normalized (mid-cycle) P/E.why: A cyclical company's profit is high at the top of its cycle and low at the bottom; a P/E on peak profit overvalues it and one on trough profit undervalues it. A mid-cycle margin evens that out.
Normalized (mid-cycle) P/E.fits: Cyclical companies (35% of their stage weight).
Normalized (mid-cycle) P/E.watch: History since 2020 may not hold a full cycle, and a lasting change in margins is treated as noise.

Normalized (mid-cycle) DCF.what: The DCF with its operating margin set to the median quarterly operating margin since 2020 instead of the latest one.
Normalized (mid-cycle) DCF.why: Projecting a peak or trough margin for five years and beyond compounds the error of the cycle; the mid-cycle margin is the better estimate of what the business earns over time.
Normalized (mid-cycle) DCF.fits: Cyclical companies (35% of their stage weight).
Normalized (mid-cycle) DCF.watch: The same limits as the normalized P/E, plus all of the DCF's sensitivity to the WACC and terminal growth.

Path-to-margin DCF.what: For a loss-making company, a DCF in which the operating margin moves in a straight line from today's to the peer median by year five, so the forecast describes a path to profit instead of assuming losses forever.
Path-to-margin DCF.why: A growing company often loses money because it is building scale. If it reaches its peers' margins, the cash after that is what it is worth; the path makes that explicit and testable.
Path-to-margin DCF.fits: Companies with an operating loss and revenue growth of 10% or more.
Path-to-margin DCF.watch: It assumes the company does reach peer margins, which many do not, and it ignores the money needed to survive the losses — the dilution-adjusted version adds that.

Path-to-margin DCF, dilution-adjusted.what: The path-to-margin DCF, with the cash the company burns before break-even assumed to be raised by selling new shares at today's price. Value per share = equity value ÷ (today's shares + the new shares).
Path-to-margin DCF, dilution-adjusted.why: Losses must be paid for. If they are funded by issuing shares, today's owners end up with a smaller slice of the eventual business; ignoring that overstates what their shares are worth.
Path-to-margin DCF, dilution-adjusted.fits: The lead method for pre-profit companies (25% of the stage weight).
Path-to-margin DCF, dilution-adjusted.watch: The money could come instead from debt, or from shares sold at a higher or lower price; a rising share price means less dilution.

Exit-multiple (venture) method.what: The venture capital method with public-market inputs: take revenue in year five on the growth path, apply the peer median operating margin and tax to get a profit, value that profit at the peer median P/E, discount it back five years at the cost of equity plus a 5-point stage premium, and divide by the diluted share count.
Exit-multiple (venture) method.why: It is how growth investors think: what will this be worth once it matures, and what return do I need for carrying the risk until then? The stage premium stands for the extra return investors demand from young, unproven companies.
Exit-multiple (venture) method.fits: Pre-profit companies with a peer P/E (20% of their stage weight).
Exit-multiple (venture) method.watch: Everything hangs on year-five revenue and on reaching peer margins. The 5-point premium is an assumption; private VCs use far higher target returns because theirs also cover failure, which here is handled separately by the survival-weighted value.

Survival-weighted value.what: A company that may fail is worth a blend of two outcomes: it survives and is worth its going-concern value, or it fails and its owners get what the assets fetch. Value = (1 − p) × the going-concern value + p × the liquidation value, where p is the probability of failing within five years: 1 − (1 − the one-year distress probability)^5 from the credit models, or, without them, a stated rule from the cash runway. The liquidation value is tangible book × 0.8, never below zero.
Survival-weighted value.why: A business that may not survive is worth the probability-weighted average of the two outcomes, not its success case. This is the First Chicago method reduced to two scenarios.
Survival-weighted value.fits: Companies burning cash (negative free cash flow) at the pre-revenue (20%), pre-profit (20%) and decline (20%) stages.
Survival-weighted value.watch: Failure probabilities are hard to estimate, and the runway rule is a rule of thumb. A forced sale can fetch less than the liquidation value assumed.

EV/Sales vs Rule of 40 (all-company fit).what: The Rule of 40 says a growth company is healthy when revenue growth % plus free-cash-flow margin % reaches 40. Across every listed non-financial company with at least $50 million of revenue, the site fits a line between the logarithm of EV/Sales and that score. This company's score gives its fitted EV/Sales (± one standard error); × revenue, minus net debt, ÷ shares, that is the value per share.
EV/Sales vs Rule of 40 (all-company fit).why: Markets pay more per dollar of sales for companies that grow fast and for companies that generate cash, and they trade the two off roughly one for one. Fitting that across the whole market prices growth without needing profits.
EV/Sales vs Rule of 40 (all-company fit).watch: One line across all industries is coarse; sectors with structurally low margins sit below it for good reasons.

Tangible book (asset value).what: Tangible book value is equity minus goodwill and intangible assets — what remains of the shareholders' money in physical and financial assets. Per share, it is an asset-value floor; the low end applies a 20% haircut for a forced sale.
Tangible book (asset value).why: When a company's future earnings are in doubt, the question becomes what its assets would fetch. Leaving out goodwill and intangibles avoids counting what cannot be sold separately.
Tangible book (asset value).watch: Book values are historical costs, not market prices; specialized assets can sell for far less, while valuable brands or patents are left out entirely.

Net cash (floor).what: Cash and investments minus debt and other claims, per diluted share, never below zero: what shareholders would own if the pipeline — the drug, technology or product still in development — turned out to be worth nothing. The market value above it is the market-implied value of the pipeline.
Net cash (floor).why: For a company with almost no revenue, the cash is the one solid number. Separating it shows how much of the price is a bet on the pipeline.
Net cash (floor).fits: Pre-revenue companies (half of their stage weight).
Net cash (floor).watch: The cash is being spent: next year's floor will be lower unless the company raises more, which dilutes.

Sum of the parts (segments × peer EV/Sal.what: Values each reported business segment separately — its revenue (latest quarter × 4) times the median EV/Sales of the industry its name maps to — adds them up, subtracts net debt and divides by diluted shares.
Sum of the parts (segments × peer EV/Sal.why: The segments of a diversified company can deserve very different multiples; a single company-wide multiple averages them away.
Sum of the parts (segments × peer EV/Sal.fits: Companies reporting two or more segments.
Sum of the parts (segments × peer EV/Sal.watch: Segment names are matched to industries automatically, and sales multiples ignore segment margins: a rough guide.

P/TBV vs ROTCE (bank peers).what: Price to tangible book (P/TBV) set against return on tangible common equity (ROTCE) across all covered banks: banks that earn more on their equity trade at higher multiples of it. The fitted line gives the P/TBV this bank's ROTCE deserves, × its tangible book per share.
P/TBV vs ROTCE (bank peers).why: For a bank, the balance sheet is the business: its value is its equity times how profitably it uses that equity, and the market's price for that profitability can be read off its peers.
P/TBV vs ROTCE (bank peers).watch: Credit quality, interest-rate risk and capital levels also move bank multiples and are not in the line.

P/B vs ROE (insurer peers).what: Price-to-book (P/B) set against return on equity (ROE) across all covered insurers; the fitted line gives the P/B this insurer's ROE deserves, × its book per share.
P/B vs ROE (insurer peers).why: An insurer's equity backs the policies it writes; its value is that equity times how profitably it underwrites and invests, which peers price.
P/B vs ROE (insurer peers).watch: Reserve adequacy, catastrophe exposure and investment risk are not in the line.

Justified P/TBV (Gordon growth).what: The P/TBV a bank deserves in theory: (ROTCE − g) ÷ (kₑ − g), where g, the sustainable growth, is ROTCE × the share of profit retained, capped at 0–4%. It is the Gordon growth model applied to book value.
Justified P/TBV (Gordon growth).why: A bank that earns exactly its cost of equity is worth its book; one that earns more is worth more, in proportion to how much more and how long it can grow.
Justified P/TBV (Gordon growth).fits: Banks with positive tangible book and ROTCE above their growth.
Justified P/TBV (Gordon growth).watch: Very sensitive when ROTCE or growth is close to the cost of equity.

Justified P/B (Gordon growth).what: The P/B an insurer deserves in theory: (ROE − g) ÷ (kₑ − g), with g = ROE × the share of profit retained, capped at 0–4%: the Gordon growth model applied to book value.
Justified P/B (Gordon growth).why: Earning exactly the cost of equity is worth book; earning more is worth more, the more so the longer it can grow.
Justified P/B (Gordon growth).fits: Insurers with positive book and ROE above their growth.
Justified P/B (Gordon growth).watch: Very sensitive when ROE or growth is close to the cost of equity.

Dividend discount (Gordon).what: The dividend discount model (DDM) values a share as next year's dividend per share (DPS) ÷ (cost of equity − growth): the Gordon growth formula for a dividend that grows forever at a constant rate.
Dividend discount (Gordon).why: For an owner who never sells, dividends are the only cash received; for steady payers they measure value directly.
Dividend discount (Gordon).fits: Banks, insurers and REITs that pay dividends.
Dividend discount (Gordon).watch: It ignores retained earnings and buybacks and breaks down when growth approaches the cost of equity.

P/FFO vs REIT peers.what: Funds from operations (FFO) is a REIT's net income plus real-estate depreciation minus gains on property sales — closer to its recurring cash earnings. The REIT is valued at the median price-to-FFO of the other covered REITs.
P/FFO vs REIT peers.why: Buildings are depreciated in the accounts even when they hold or gain value, so net income understates a REIT's earnings; FFO, as defined by Nareit, is the industry's standard measure.
P/FFO vs REIT peers.fits: REITs with positive FFO (55% of their stage weight).
P/FFO vs REIT peers.watch: Property types (offices, data centers, apartments) trade at very different multiples; one REIT median blends them.

Stage-weighted value.what: The combination: each method the company's stage uses, × its weight (renormalized over the methods this company has), summed into one value.
Stage-weighted value.why: Averaging methods with different blind spots reduces the error of any single one. Fixing the weights in advance, by stage, prevents choosing whichever method flatters the stock.
Stage-weighted value.fits: Every company with a stage and at least one of its methods.
Stage-weighted value.watch: The weights are judgments; the football field shows every method so you can weigh them yourself.

Analysts' price targets.what: The 12-month price targets of the Wall Street analysts who cover the stock (mean and range), from Yahoo Finance's consensus.
Analysts' price targets.why: Shown as an outside opinion to compare against, not as a valuation: targets come without their assumptions.
Analysts' price targets.watch: Targets tend to follow the share price and lean optimistic on average.

Polymarket implied price.what: Polymarket is a prediction market where people bet on outcomes, including ranges for where a stock will close by a date. The price of each range contract reads as the crowd's probability; combined, they give the price the crowd expects.
Polymarket implied price.why: Shown as the crowd's forecast, a check on the models, not as a valuation.
Polymarket implied price.fits: Stocks with active Polymarket price markets.
Polymarket implied price.watch: Thin markets can be moved by a few traders, and they forecast a price, not a value.

Our model.what: The site's own price forecasts from its rotation and combined models, recorded in the forecast ledger before the outcome is known and scored walk-forward against what happened.
Our model.why: Shown so the models' forecasts can be compared with the valuations and held to account.
Our model.watch: A forecast of the price over months, not an estimate of value; check its track record in the ledger.

52-week trading range.what: The lowest and highest closing prices of the past 52 weeks: where the market itself has priced the company recently.
52-week trading range.why: A reminder of how much the price alone has moved, against which the methods' spread can be judged.
52-week trading range.watch: Not a valuation: a range of past prices.

Graham number.what: Benjamin Graham's ceiling for a defensive investor: the square root of 22.5 × earnings per share × book value per share. 22.5 is 15 × 1.5 — Graham would pay at most 15 times earnings and 1.5 times book, and the product lets a lower P/E make room for a higher P/B.
Graham number.why: It asks for two things at once — real earnings and real assets — and refuses to pay much for either. A price far above it is a bet on growth or on assets the books do not show.
Graham number.fits: Profitable companies with positive book value, above all steady, asset-heavy ones.
Graham number.watch: It ignores growth and intangible assets entirely, so almost every fast-growing or asset-light company looks expensive by it; buybacks that shrink book value make it fall.

Graham formula (revised).what: Graham's formula from The Intelligent Investor, revised in 1974: value = EPS × (8.5 + 2g) × 4.4 ÷ Y. 8.5 is the P/E he gave a company that does not grow, g the expected yearly growth in percent, 4.4 the AAA corporate bond yield of 1962 and Y the AAA yield today — so higher interest rates lower the value.
Graham formula (revised).why: It is the simplest growth-and-rates valuation there is: it prices growth linearly and scales everything by what safe corporate bonds pay instead.
Graham formula (revised).fits: Profitable companies with a believable growth estimate.
Graham formula (revised).watch: Growth enters linearly, so it overvalues fast growers — growth is capped at 15% here. Graham himself warned it is a rough guide, not a precise value.

Net current asset value (net-net).what: Current assets (cash, receivables, inventory) minus every liability, long-term debt included, divided by the shares: what shareholders would keep if the factories, brands and the business itself were worth nothing. Graham bought 'net-nets' below two-thirds of this figure.
Net current asset value (net-net).why: It is the hardest floor there is: a company trading below it is priced as if it were worth less dead than its working capital alone.
Net current asset value (net-net).fits: Industrial companies with a working-capital-heavy balance sheet; rare among large companies today.
Net current asset value (net-net).watch: Inventory and receivables may not fetch book value in a liquidation, and a company losing money burns the working capital that makes the floor. Negative for most companies financed with long-term debt — that is normal, not a warning.

Lynch fair P/E (PEGY).what: Peter Lynch's rule: a fairly priced company's P/E equals its growth rate (in percent) — the PEG ratio of 1 — and a dividend counts like growth (PEGY = P/E ÷ (growth + yield)). Value here = EPS × (growth + dividend yield, in percent), with the fair P/E kept between 5 and 40.
Lynch fair P/E (PEGY).why: It ties the multiple to what the earnings will do, which a plain P/E comparison does not.
Lynch fair P/E (PEGY).fits: Profitable companies with a growth estimate, from slow growers paying dividends to fast growers.
Lynch fair P/E (PEGY).watch: A rule of thumb with no cash flows behind it: it ignores the cost of capital, how long growth lasts and how much reinvestment it needs. Analysts' growth looks one or two years ahead; Lynch meant several.

Earnings power value (EPV).what: Bruce Greenwald's earnings power value: the value of the business as it is today if it never grew. Operating profit at its average margin over the cycle × today's revenue, after tax, plus depreciation less the capital spending needed only to stand still, divided by the cost of capital, less net debt.
Earnings power value (EPV).why: It strips out every forecast of growth, so the gap between the price and EPV is exactly what the market pays for growth. EPV above the cost of rebuilding the assets (tangible book) points to a competitive advantage.
Earnings power value (EPV).fits: Companies with an operating profit over the cycle, above all mature and cyclical ones.
Earnings power value (EPV).watch: Splitting capital spending into upkeep and growth is an estimate (here from PP&E ÷ revenue × last year's revenue gain). A margin average over a few years may not be a full cycle.

FCFE DCF (cash to shareholders).what: A discounted cash flow from the shareholders' side: free cash flow to equity = net income − the part of reinvestment (capex − depreciation + working capital) that shareholders fund, the rest being borrowed at a steady debt ratio — discounted at the cost of equity, with a terminal value of earnings less the reinvestment growth needs.
FCFE DCF (cash to shareholders).why: It values the cash that can actually be paid out to owners and complements the enterprise DCF, which discounts cash to all funders at the WACC.
FCFE DCF (cash to shareholders).fits: Profitable companies with positive equity and a stable debt ratio.
FCFE DCF (cash to shareholders).watch: Sensitive to the cost of equity and to leverage: a company that borrows more shows more cash to equity today and more risk tomorrow.

H-model dividend discount.what: A dividend discount model in which dividend growth falls in a straight line from today's rate to the long-run rate over 2H years (here 10): value = D₀ × [(1 + g_L) + H × (g_S − g_L)] ÷ (kₑ − g_L). Fuller and Hsia (1984).
H-model dividend discount.why: Dividends do not grow fast forever, nor drop to the economy's pace overnight; the H-model spreads the slowdown over a decade with one closed formula.
H-model dividend discount.fits: Companies that pay a dividend which can keep growing for a while.
H-model dividend discount.watch: Only dividends count, so a company paying out little and buying back shares looks cheap by nothing; short-term growth is capped at 10%.

Real option to expand.what: Values the chance to grow into a bigger business like a call option (Black-Scholes): the underlying is today's value of the expansion — the revenue it adds by year five at a mature margin — the strike is the capital it takes to build it, the volatility is the stock's own. Value = the business in place + the option − net debt.
Real option to expand.why: For a loss-making or fast-growing company a plain DCF of the expected path misses that management can stop if things go badly and push on if they go well; uncertainty makes such a choice more valuable, not less.
Real option to expand.watch: Black-Scholes assumes a traded underlying and a fixed strike; the stock's volatility stands in for the project's. Read it as a sense of how much flexibility could be worth, not as a precise value.

EV/Sales fair multiple (multi-factor fit.what: A regression across every covered non-financial company of ln(EV/Sales) on revenue growth, the log of the operating margin (EV/Sales = EV/EBIT × margin), a loss flag, size and sector: the multiple the market pays, today, for a company with this one's growth, margin, size and sector.
EV/Sales fair multiple (multi-factor fit.why: Unlike a plain peer median it adjusts for how this company differs from its peers, and unlike a DCF it uses the market's own pricing.
EV/Sales fair multiple (multi-factor fit.fits: Non-financial companies with revenue of $50 million or more.
EV/Sales fair multiple (multi-factor fit.watch: It inherits the market's mood: if every company is dear, the fit is dear too. The range (± one residual standard error) is wide — companies with the same figures trade at very different multiples.
